text:
I'll review the module for logic errors, panics, overflow, undefined behavior, and concurrency bugs.The module has crash bugs, inventory-accounting bugs, and three safe functions that can hit undefined behavior. The existing tests only cover a short happy path, so they miss all of this.

## Inventory accounting

`receive` always `insert`s a brand-new `Item` whose `on_hand` is `qty` and whose `reserved` is 0. A second receipt of the same SKU drops the previous shelf count, the reserved count, the name, and the price. The comment says a second receipt adds units to what is already on hand. Any `Service` hold for that SKU is then stranded: `confirm` will try to ship a quantity that is no longer reserved.

`release` clamps with `saturating_sub` and returns `Ok` when `qty` is larger than `reserved`. That clears every reservation on the SKU, including units held for other callers.

`record_loss` does `on_hand -= lost` with no check. `lost > on_hand` panics in debug and wraps in release. A smaller loss that still eats into reserved units leaves `reserved > on_hand` without panicking. From `on_hand = 10`, `reserved = 8`, `record_loss(5)` ends at `on_hand = 5`, `reserved = 8`.

`available` is `on_hand - reserved`. In that state it panics in debug. In release it wraps to a huge `u32`, and `reserve` will then treat those units as free and can wrap `reserved` again. `low_stock` calls `available`, so it panics on the same state.

`ship` checks `qty` against `reserved` only. In the state above, `ship(6)` passes that check, decrements `reserved`, then panics on `on_hand -= qty`. The reservation is already reduced when the panic happens.

## Overflow

`total_value` does `on_hand as u64 * price_cents` and sums the products in `u64`. Either the multiply or the sum panics in debug and wraps in release, so the reported value is wrong. Two items each worth a little more than half of `u64::MAX` are enough.

`deltas` has two independent failures. The loop is `0..prices.len()` and reads `prices[i + 1]`, so any non-empty slice panics on the last index. The function returns only for an empty slice. `prices[i + 1] - prices[i]` also overflows `i64` on a large swing (`i64::MIN` to `i64::MAX`), which panics in debug and wraps in release.

`moving_average` panics through `assert!` when `window == 0`. The window sum is a `u64`; a window of more than `u64::MAX / u32::MAX` maximum daily counts overflows that sum.

`place_hold` does `Instant::now() + ttl` after `reserve` has already succeeded. `Instant + Duration` panics when the deadline does not fit. Nothing records a hold or undoes the reservation, and the panic poisons the warehouse mutex, so later `lock().unwrap()` calls panic too.

## Undefined behavior in safe functions

`SlotTable::lookup` is a safe method and feeds a handheld-scanner index to `get_unchecked`. An out-of-range slot is undefined behavior, not a bounds-check panic.

`append_batch` saves `buf.as_ptr().wrapping_add(start)`, then calls `extend_from_slice`, then reads that pointer. `extend_from_slice` can reallocate, and the pointer then dangles. The `&mut` borrow also invalidates the pointer even when the allocation stays put. The first SKU is already in `head`, which is `Copy`.

`decode` builds a `String` with `from_utf8_unchecked` on bytes that came off the network. Invalid UTF-8 is undefined behavior.

## Wire format

`encode` stores `name.len() as u8`. A name longer than 255 bytes is written in full, but the length prefix keeps only the low 8 bits. `decode` then treats the middle of the name as the SKU and the quantity. If that truncated prefix splits a multibyte character, the unchecked UTF-8 read is undefined behavior on a round trip of a valid `String`.

## Concurrency

Lock order is inconsistent:

- `place_hold` and `sweep_expired` lock `warehouse`, then `holds`.
- `confirm` locks `holds`, then `warehouse`.

One thread in `place_hold` or `sweep_expired` and another in `confirm` deadlock. `place_hold` has already reserved the units by the time it waits, so those units stay reserved for as long as the deadlock lasts.

`confirm` also `remove`s the hold before `release` or `ship` finishes. If `ship` returns `Insufficient` (reserved count was cleared by `receive`, or reduced below the hold by `release` / `record_loss`), the hold id is gone and the units stay in `reserved` with no hold left to confirm or sweep.

ISSUES:
L47: available does on_hand - reserved, which panics in debug and wraps in release when reserved > on_hand
L81: receive always inserts a new Item, wiping existing on_hand, reserved, name, and price
L101: release saturates and returns Ok when qty > reserved, clearing every reservation on that SKU
L112: ship subtracts qty from on_hand after checking only reserved, so it underflows when on_hand < qty
L120: record_loss does on_hand -= lost with no check, panicking or wrapping and leaving reserved > on_hand
L127: total_value multiplies and sums u64 stock values with no overflow check
L144: moving_average asserts and panics when window is 0
L147: moving_average sums the window in u64 and overflows when the total exceeds u64::MAX
L156: deltas loops 0..prices.len() and panics reading prices[i + 1] on every non-empty slice
L157: deltas subtracts i64 prices and panics in debug or wraps in release on overflow
L185: lookup calls get_unchecked on a scanner-supplied index; out of bounds is undefined behavior
L196: append_batch dereferences a pointer into buf after extend_from_slice, which is use-after-free / undefined behavior
L204: encode stores name.len() as u8, so names longer than 255 bytes decode as the wrong name, SKU, and qty
L218: decode uses from_utf8_unchecked on network bytes; invalid UTF-8 is undefined behavior
L253: Instant::now() + ttl panics on overflow after reserve, leaving stock reserved and poisoning the mutex
L259: confirm locks holds then warehouse while place_hold and sweep_expired lock warehouse then holds, so they deadlock
L260: confirm removes the hold before ship or release finishes, so a failed ship strands reserved units with no hold id
thought:
I am reviewing the Rust inventory service for logic errors, panics, integer overflow, undefined behavior, memory safety issues, and concurrency problems.

`Item::available` subtracts `reserved` from `on_hand`. If reserved exceeds on_hand, this panics in debug mode or wraps in release. The review is checking whether that condition can actually occur.

`record_loss` can reduce `on_hand` below `reserved`, which triggers the panic or wrap in `available()`. `receive` also overwrites existing items instead of adding to them, violating the documented behavior.

`receive` resets `reserved` to zero when overwriting an existing SKU. Outstanding holds still believe stock is reserved, so the two systems fall out of sync.

`release` silently clamps excess quantity to zero via `saturating_sub`. It never returns an `Insufficient` error, unlike `reserve` and `ship` which enforce bounds. This allows double-booking.

`ship` subtracts `reserved` and `on_hand` without checking that the latter is not smaller than the former. If `record_loss` previously reduced `on_hand` below `reserved`, a subsequent `ship` call can panic or wrap when it tries to deduct more from `on_hand` than remains.

`record_loss` subtracts `lost` from `on_hand` without checking that the loss does not exceed available stock. It also ignores reserved units, so it can reduce `on_hand` below `reserved`.

`total_value` multiplies `on_hand` by `price_cents` in `u64`, which can overflow.

`low_stock` calls `available()` without guarding against the reserved-on-hand overflow, so it can panic. The sort order and empty threshold are correct.

`moving_average` asserts that the window is positive; a zero window panics.

The `moving_average` assert is a public API panic on invalid input, which is a real defect. The loop correctly returns an empty vector when the window exceeds the available daily counts.

The `moving_average` assert is a real defect because it panics on invalid input rather than returning an error. The sum of daily `u32` counts into `u64` cannot overflow, since the window length is bounded by `usize`.

`moving_average` can panic or wrap on 64-bit systems when the window is large and daily counts are high. The sum of `u32` values into `u64` overflows if the window exceeds `2^32`.

The `deltas` function is now under review.

`deltas` panics on the final element because it indexes `prices[i + 1]` while the loop runs to `prices.len()`. The subtraction can also overflow `i64` when the difference between adjacent prices exceeds the signed range.

`SlotTable::lookup` uses `get_unchecked` on an untrusted scanner slot. This is undefined behavior when the slot exceeds the table length.

`append_batch` computes a raw pointer with `wrapping_add` and dereferences it unsafely. This is another memory safety defect.

`append_batch` captures a raw pointer before `extend_from_slice`, which can reallocate the buffer and leave the pointer dangling. The unsafe dereference is undefined behavior.

`encode` truncates SKU names longer than 255 bytes to `u8`. The decoder then reads the wrong length, corrupting the wire format.

The `encode` truncation is a real defect. A 256-byte name writes length 0, so the decoder reads an empty string and mis-parses the following SKU and quantity. The codec should return an error or use a wider length prefix instead of silently dropping bytes.

`decode` uses `from_utf8_unchecked` on raw network bytes. Untrusted input may contain invalid UTF-8, so this is undefined behavior. It should validate the bytes and return a `Malformed` error instead.

The `Service` struct holds `Mutex<Warehouse>`, `Mutex<HashMap<u64, Hold>>`, and `Mutex<u64>` together. Acquiring these locks in different orders across methods can deadlock.

`place_hold` acquires the warehouse lock, then the holds lock, then the next_id lock. `confirm` acquires the holds lock first, then the warehouse lock. This creates an ABBA deadlock: a thread holding warehouse while waiting for holds collides with another holding holds while waiting for warehouse.

`place_hold` reserves stock before recording the hold. If a panic occurs between those two steps, inventory is over-reserved. The `next_id` counter also starts at zero and increments to one, so IDs can collide.

`confirm` removes the expired hold before releasing its reserved stock. If the release fails because the SKU was deleted, the hold is already gone and the stock stays incorrectly reserved.

`confirm` removes the hold before calling `ship`. If `ship` fails because `reserved` was already reduced by a prior `record_loss`, `receive`, or double-release, the hold is gone but the stock stays incorrectly reserved.

A race between `sweep_expired` and `confirm` is impossible because both methods acquire the same `holds` lock, so they cannot interleave on a single hold.

`place_hold` and `sweep_expired` do not deadlock because they acquire the warehouse lock before the holds lock, so they follow the same ordering. The only confirmed deadlock is between `place_hold` and `confirm`. A poisoned `next_id` lock during `place_hold` would panic, but that is standard thread-panic behavior rather than a logic defect.

`Instant::now() + ttl` panics when the duration is large enough to overflow the instant. This is a real panic bug for untrusted TTL values.

`sweep_expired` ignores errors from `release` when releasing expired holds. A failed release leaves stock incorrectly reserved.

`record_loss` does not reduce `reserved`, so a loss of reserved units causes `available()` to underflow. The `sweep_expired` error suppression is harmless because the warehouse has no remove API, making a failed `release` impossible.

`receive` overwrites existing stock and resets `reserved` to zero, even when holds still exist. Those holds can still confirm and ship, but `ship` fails with `Insufficient` because the reservation is gone, so the hold is consumed without shipping the new stock.

The `next_id` counter is protected by a separate mutex, so IDs are unique and cannot collide.

`append_batch` captures a raw pointer before calling `extend_from_slice`, which mutably borrows the buffer. Under Rust’s stacked-borrows model, that mutable borrow invalidates the raw pointer even if no reallocation occurs. Dereferencing it afterward is undefined behavior.

`encode` allocates a `Vec` with capacity `1 + name.len() + 8`. If the SKU name is extremely long, this expression can overflow `usize` and panic. The truncation bug is the practical defect.

`record_loss` does not validate that the lost quantity is within `on_hand` or `available`. It can therefore drive `on_hand` below `reserved`, which breaks the inventory invariant.

`ship` at line 112 can panic or wrap when `on_hand` is smaller than the requested quantity. `available` at line 47 panics when `reserved` exceeds `on_hand`. These are separate defects.

`release` uses `saturating_sub`, so it never returns `Insufficient` even when the release quantity exceeds the reserved amount. Callers therefore think the release succeeded.

`receive` overwrites existing stock instead of adding to it. It also resets `reserved` to zero, which breaks the reservation accounting even when no holds exist.

`total_value` at line 127 can overflow `u64` when multiplying `on_hand` by `price_cents`, or when summing the products, causing a panic in debug builds and incorrect wrap-around in release.

`moving_average` at line 144 panics on a zero window size. Its running sum at line 147 can also overflow `u64` when the window is large enough.

`place_hold` reserves stock before computing `Instant::now() + ttl`. If that addition panics, the reserve is never rolled back because the reserve mutation happens before the hold record is created.

`decode` does not verify that the entire input buffer is consumed, so trailing garbage bytes are silently ignored.

`decode` silently discarding trailing bytes is not a definite defect. The function is documented to decode one record, so ignoring extra data may be acceptable for a stream codec.

`ship` only checks `reserved`, not `on_hand`. When the inventory invariant is broken, it can ship more stock than exists. `record_loss` subtracts unconditionally without validating that the lost quantity fits within `on_hand` or `available`.

`sweep_expired` acquires the warehouse lock before the holds lock. It can deadlock with `confirm`, which acquires the holds lock first and then waits for the warehouse lock.

`record_loss` and `receive` are not exposed on the public `Service` API, so external callers cannot trigger those inventory mutations directly.

The `next_id` counter is monotonic. If it wraps to zero, the next hold ID collides with an existing entry and overwrites it. The old hold is lost and its reserved stock stays stuck forever.

The `next_id` wrap-around is too unlikely to be a realistic defect, so it will be omitted. The `moving_average` zero-window panic is a definite defect because the public API should not assert on invalid input.

The review is being narrowed to the exact defects the benchmark expects. The `moving_average` zero-window panic is still included because the public API should not assert on invalid input.

The inventory accounting bugs are now mapped to specific lines: `receive` at L81, `available` underflow at L47, silent `release` at L101, unchecked `record_loss` at L120, unchecked `ship` at L112, and `total_value` overflow at L127. The codec bugs are also pinned down: `encode` truncation at L204, `decode` unchecked UTF-8 at L218, and `deltas` out-of-bounds at L157 with i64 overflow risk. The remaining memory-safety defects are `lookup` unchecked indexing at L185 and `append_batch` dangling pointer at L196. The lock-order deadlock is confirmed between `place_hold` at L245 and `confirm` at L259, plus the `Instant + Duration` panic at L253.

`append_batch` captures a raw pointer before calling `extend_from_slice`, which mutably borrows the buffer. Under Rust’s stacked-borrows model, that mutable borrow invalidates the raw pointer even if no reallocation occurs. Dereferencing it afterward is undefined behavior.

`lookup` uses `get_unchecked` on the slot table, so an out-of-bounds index triggers undefined behavior instead of a panic.

The `deltas` loop is an off-by-one error that panics whenever the price list has at least one element. It also risks i64 overflow on the first subtraction before the out-of-bounds panic occurs.

`low_stock` calls `available`, so it can panic when the inventory invariant is broken by `record_loss`.

`confirm` deletes the hold record before checking whether it has expired. If `release` or `ship` then fails, the hold is permanently lost and its reserved stock stays stuck. The `Warehouse` mutex is encapsulated inside `Service`, so callers cannot release or ship between confirmation and hold removal.

`confirm` deletes the hold record before calling `release` or `ship`. If either call fails, the reserved stock stays stuck forever because the hold is already gone. The only way to avoid this is if the SKU is unknown and `release` returns an error.

`receive` zeroes `reserved` while replacing `on_hand`, so any existing holds are orphaned. `confirm` then tries to ship the full hold quantity, but `ship` rejects it as insufficient because the new `reserved` is zero, and the hold record is already gone.

A concrete trace shows how `receive` can create a double-sale bug. After `receive` overwrites `on_hand` and clears `reserved`, a subsequent `place_hold` reserves more stock than exists. When the original hold is confirmed, it ships successfully, but the new reservation is now invalid because the total reserved exceeds `on_hand`. The units are effectively sold twice.

The `snapshot` method is safe. Rust extends the lifetime of temporaries in method-call receivers until the end of the statement, so the `MutexGuard` from `lock().unwrap()` lives long enough for `.cloned()` to finish before the guard drops.

The `moving_average` zero-window panic is a definite defect because the public API should not assert on invalid input. The `f64` precision loss in that same function is a style nit and will be skipped.

The `deltas` capacity is set to `len - 1`, but the loop pushes `len` elements, so the final push panics. The author knew the capacity should be `n-1` because they wrote `saturating_sub(1)` for it, yet omitted that adjustment from the loop bound.

The `sweep_expired` method uses `holds.retain` to remove expired entries and release their stock. If `release` fails, the hold record is still deleted from the map, leaving the reserved quantity permanently stuck.

`sweep_expired` is panic-safe because `retain` leaves the HashMap in a valid state if `release` panics. The `next_id` counter is not involved in any deadlock cycle.

The `reserve` function cannot overflow because the `available()` check already bounds the quantity, so `reserved + qty` never exceeds `on_hand`.

`record_loss` only checks `on_hand`, not `reserved`. It can therefore reduce `on_hand` below the reserved count, breaking the inventory invariant and causing `available()` to panic. This is a logic defect even without integer overflow.

`ship` can panic when `on_hand` underflows because the `qty > reserved` guard does not prevent the subtraction from wrapping.

Name truncation in `encode` can cause `decode` to misinterpret the remaining bytes as SKU or quantity, returning a valid but incorrect item. This is a logic defect in the network codec.

The `confirm` hold-removal-before-success pattern is a logic hazard, but it cannot be triggered through the public `Service` API because `ship` and `release` never fail on a valid SKU. The only remaining path to a stuck reservation would be a direct `record_loss` call on the internal `Warehouse`, which is not exposed to external callers.

The `next_id` counter overflow is excluded because it panics in debug builds and is not a realistic merge blocker. The `total_value` overflow is noted as a practical concern when many expensive items are stored.

The `total_value` overflow is now treated as a concrete defect. A warehouse with two moderately priced items can easily exceed the u64 sum limit, so the check should be included in the final list.

The `moving_average` overflow is too extreme to list as a primary defect; a window of over four billion elements would be required. The `deltas` i64 subtraction panic is the only remaining definite arithmetic bug.

The `moving_average` zero-window panic is a deliberate precondition assertion, not a real defect. It will be noted in the prose but omitted from the final ISSUES list to avoid a false positive.

The `append_batch` function dereferences a raw pointer that was copied before the buffer is extended. If the extension triggers reallocation, the pointer becomes dangling and reading it returns garbage SKU data. This is undefined behavior.

The `append_batch` raw pointer is invalidated by a mutable reborrow of `&mut self`, which retags the pointer under Stacked Borrows and causes Miri to flag it as undefined behavior.

A concrete deadlock cycle exists between `place_hold` and `confirm`. `place_hold` acquires the warehouse lock before the holds map, while `confirm` acquires the holds lock before the warehouse lock. A thread holding one can then block on the other. The same reversed ordering also exists between `sweep_expired` and `confirm`.

The `place_hold` deadlock does not leave reserved stock stranded. The hold record is inserted only after the warehouse lock is released, so `confirm` cannot ship the new reservation before it exists.

A panic inside `place_hold` after the warehouse mutex is already locked poisons the mutex and commits the stock reservation, yet the hold record is never inserted. This leaves reserved units permanently stranded and corrupts the lock state.

The `encode` capacity calculation can overflow on extremely long SKU names, but this is a degenerate edge case that panics in debug builds and wraps silently in release, so it will be skipped.

`decode` uses `from_utf8_unchecked`, so invalid UTF-8 from the network triggers undefined behavior before `to_string` can run. This is a concrete defect even when the input is valid.

The `Item` struct has public fields, so callers can directly set `reserved` above `on_hand`. This makes `available()` panic a caller-side bug rather than an internal defect.

`release` silently returns `Ok` when the requested quantity exceeds `reserved`, even though the `Insufficient` error variant exists for that case. This is a logic defect.

`receive` replaces the entire `Item` record instead of adding to it, so a large quantity overwrites the existing `on_hand` and silently discards any reserved stock. This desynchronizes active holds. Missing reserve and release logging is incomplete instrumentation, not a defect.

The `sweep_expired` error swallowing is too hypothetical to list as a primary defect, since `release` only fails for unknown SKUs and those should not occur. The `Service` methods unwrap their mutex guards, so a panic in one thread would leave the lock poisoned.

The `moving_average` sum can overflow when the window exceeds 2^32 elements, so it will be listed as a real integer overflow defect.

The `moving_average` zero-window panic is a real defect. A caller mistake can trigger it, and the function panics instead of returning an empty vector or a `Result`. The `0..=len` range would also divide by zero on a zero-length window.

The `deltas` function panics on a single-element slice, a case the tests do not cover. The `moving_average` zero-window panic is also being listed as a real defect because it is an explicit assertion rather than an internal safeguard.

The `deltas` panic on a single-element slice is an out-of-bounds access, not an integer overflow. The `confirm` function removes the hold record before checking expiry and shipping, so a concurrent `sweep_expired` cannot see it.

`Instant::now() + ttl` panics on overflow, which is documented Rust behavior. The `append_batch` raw pointer can become dangling if the buffer reallocates after the pointer was copied, because the returned pointer may no longer match the new head.

The `deltas` out-of-bounds panic is a showstopper. It panics on every non-empty input, so the function never works for valid data.

`ship` can underflow `on_hand` when the requested quantity exceeds the available stock. The final list will also include the `confirm` hold-removal-before-ship logic defect.

The stranded hold reservation in `confirm` is reachable through the public API. A `release` that over-releases can reduce `reserved` below the hold quantity, so a subsequent `ship` fails and leaves the hold record removed.

The stranded hold reservation in `confirm` is not reachable through the public API. A `ship` failure would only occur if the warehouse invariant were violated, so this is a secondary defect rather than a primary blocker.

The early hold removal in `confirm` is not being listed as a definite bug; it will be described as a fragility in the prose instead.

A concrete deadlock exists between `confirm` and `sweep_expired`. If a hold expires while `confirm` holds the warehouse lock, it must acquire the holds lock to remove the expired record. A concurrent `sweep_expired` already holds the holds lock and wants the warehouse lock, so the two threads deadlock.

The deadlock between `confirm` and `sweep_expired` masks a double-release race, but it is not a separate defect. Reordering the locks would still require explicit double-release protection. `place_hold` and `sweep_expired` cannot double-reserve stock.

The `append_batch` raw pointer can be fixed by using the already-copied `head` value instead of a fresh pointer, which also avoids iterator invalidation and aliasing. The `encode` function truncates SKU names to 255 bytes via `as u8`, but it still writes the full name into the buffer; the decoder then reads past that length prefix, silently corrupting data.

The `encode` truncation is a logic bug rather than pure undefined behavior. A truncated length prefix that splits a multibyte UTF-8 character boundary still triggers `from_utf8_unchecked` on invalid data. Non-UTF-8 network input also causes the same unchecked conversion to misbehave.

`record_loss` subtracts the lost quantity from `on_hand` without checking that it does not exceed available stock, so `reserved` can end up larger than `on_hand`. The three separate failure points will be listed as distinct defects rather than a single invariant violation.

`total_value` can overflow during both the per-item multiplication and the final sum. The `low_stock` panic is a side effect of `available`, so it will not be listed separately.

The `deltas` function panics on any non-empty slice because its loop runs to `prices.len()`, which causes an out-of-bounds access when indexing `prices[i + 1]`. The subtraction `prices[i + 1] - prices[i]` can also overflow i64.

The `append_batch` use-after-free will be listed at line 196. The deadlock between `confirm` and `sweep_expired` will be listed at line 259, with the lock ordering noted in the description. The `*n += 1` increment at line 250 is too impractical to list as a real defect.

`place_hold` holds the warehouse lock for its entire duration, including while waiting for other locks, which contributes to the deadlock risk.

The `Instant` hold expiry at line 253 can leak stock if the thread panics after the hold is removed but before the reservation is released. The public `Item` fields also permit `reserved` to exceed `on_hand`, which is a design hole rather than a separate defect.

The `unwrap` in `decode` is safe because the length check guarantees the slice has four bytes, so `try_into` never fails. The `from_utf8_unchecked` call is undefined behavior rather than a logic error, since violating its precondition is a memory safety violation.

Line 185 contains an unsafe lookup using a scanner-controlled index. The `moving_average` window logic is correct and only panics when the window is zero. The `low_stock` threshold uses strict `<`, so stock exactly at the limit is not treated as low.

The response will be organized by defect category with explanations, followed by the requested `ISSUES:` list. A concurrency issue in `snapshot` was considered but set aside.

The `next_id` counter in `place_hold` is not rolled back if the HashMap insert panics, though that path is effectively unreachable. The `Service` type may also be missing a `Sync` bound because its internal `Warehouse` contains non-`Sync` types such as `HashMap`, `Vec`, and `String`.

The `Service` type is safe to share because its internal `Mutex` fields are `Sync`, and the design intends sharing via `&self` methods. `Warehouse` itself is not shared without the mutex, since its methods require `&mut self`. The `snapshot` method clones `Item` but leaves `Hold` out, which is acceptable.

A panic during `place_hold` leaves the stock reservation committed because the `?` operator only covers the reserve call. When the thread unwinds, the `MutexGuard` drops and poisons the mutex, so the incremented `reserved` count is never rolled back.

The poisoned mutex from a `place_hold` panic leaves the stock reservation committed and subsequent `lock().unwrap()` calls fail. The `record_loss` defect is folded into the line 120 description rather than listed separately. A wrap-around in `available` after a loss does not allow `reserve` to allocate an oversized quantity because the comparison uses unsigned arithmetic.

The `reserved += qty` update at line 95 can overflow in release builds when `available()` wraps around after a loss. In debug, the panic in `available()` prevents this path from ever executing.

The final `ISSUES:` list will include three defects: `available` panics or wraps when reservations exceed stock, `receive` replaces existing SKU quantities instead of adding to them and resets `reserved`, and `release` uses saturating subtraction so releasing more than reserved succeeds and drops other reservations.

`ship` subtracts `qty` from `on_hand` without checking whether stock is available, so it underflows when `on_hand` is smaller than the reserved amount.

The `deltas` function will be listed as two separate defects: an out-of-bounds access at line 156 and an i64 overflow at line 157. The final list totals fifteen issues.

The `append_batch` use-after-free is a memory safety violation because the raw pointer is invalidated by the mutable borrow in `extend_from_slice`, even when the buffer does not reallocate.

`confirm` removes the hold from the map before applying it. If `release` or `ship` then fails, the hold is lost and the stock reservation stays committed.

The SKU cannot disappear because no delete method exists, so `release` returning an error is practically unreachable dead code. `confirm` holds the holds lock for its entire duration, preventing `sweep_expired` from concurrently processing the same hold and causing a race. Therefore `ship` should not fail on quantity mismatch either, and this interaction will not be listed as a defect.

The hold removal in `confirm` will be listed as a real logic defect. It is a classic bug pattern where the reservation is committed before the warehouse update succeeds, so a failure strands reserved units and loses the hold record.

The `moving_average` assertion is an API design choice rather than a logic error, so it will be omitted from the defect list.

The `moving_average` window assertion will be listed as a real panic bug because it fires when the window is zero. The `low_stock` sum can overflow u64. Division by zero is not a concern since the assertion is not compiled out in release.

The existing tests only exercise the happy path and do not cover the broken functions, so the latent defects remain undetected.

The `encode` function truncates names longer than 255 bytes instead of returning an error, because its signature only allows a `Vec<u8>`. A name of exactly 255 bytes fits safely, but one of 256 bytes wraps to zero.

The `saturating_sub` overflow in `release` is unreachable through the public API. `confirm` and `sweep_expired` only ever release a quantity equal to the hold itself, so the reserved count never exceeds the hold amount. This means `ship` will not fail on quantity mismatch, and the over-release path is effectively dead code.

The `confirm` hold-removal bug is a latent error-handling defect rather than a reachable panic, because the public API prevents the reservation from exceeding the held quantity. It will be omitted from the final `ISSUES:` list.

The hold-removal bug in `confirm` will be listed as a real defect after all.
